newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel intervenes in shekel trading.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel intervenes in shekel trading.

text.p: The Bank of Israel intervened in the trading of the shekel on Tuesday by buying dollars, preventing the shekel from trading beyond the band within which it is allowed to fluctuate, dealers said.

"At the end of the trading day, after the representative rates were published, the central bank intervened and bought a few million dollars bringing the shekel rate against the basket (of foreign currencies) to 7.0 percent below the slope," said Israel Sapir, chief dealer at Bank Leumi.
The shekel can fluctuate in a trading band of 7.0 percent above or below a slope designed to devalue the Israeli currency at six percent a year against the basket of key currencies.
If the shekel-basket exchange rate reaches the lower trading band the market believes the central bank would intervene by buying foreign currency.

Sapir said that the shekel had been trading at 6.96 percent below the slope at the end of the day and after the representative rates were published, in trading between the banks the rate fell below 7.0 percent. Just before the central bank closed its trading day it intervened in the market and bought a small amount of dollars, Sapir said.

"The Bank of Israel brought the rate to 7.0 percent below the slope and this means it will have to intervene again tomorrow," said Sapir. "All in all this is not a change in the trend, but an intervention that had to happen."

He said that the central bank had not intervened in the market for six months. "I don't think rates will shoot up tomorrow, maybe go up slightly more because the public may think the central bank wants to weaken the shekel. But this is certainly not a change in direction."
The central bank does not confirm interventions of this sort.
